summary: A 1968 paper on binary message forms in computer networks. It argues that although the content and form of messages between computers cannot easily be standardised, a standard way of describing message forms could help, in the way ALGOL is used to describe algorithms.

eli5.summary: Different computers write messages in different shapes. This paper suggests a common way to describe those shapes so people can understand each other.

questions: binary message forms in computer networks
subtitle: A standard notation for describing binary message and data formats

tldr.problem: Different computers on the network used incompatible ways to represent binary data, and there was no standard way to document and describe these formats so others could understand them.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC proposes a symbolic description language for binary messages, inspired by BNF for language syntax, with notation for fields, values, alternatives, repetition, and conditional content.
tldr.outcome: The paper helped establish the idea that message formats need explicit, standardized documentation. Later specifications adopted similar approaches, though different formal notations eventually prevailed.

today: This 1968 paper established the importance of formal message format documentation. While the specific notation proposed here gave way to other approaches (ASN.1, XDR, Protocol Buffers, etc.), the fundamental principle—that binary formats need explicit documentation—remains essential to modern networking and data exchange.

sections.title: The Problem and the Approach
sections.content:
Network communication between computers was becoming common by 1968, but each installation had its own approach to message formats. Standardizing the content of messages seemed impossible given the diversity of systems and purposes. However, a standard way of describing message forms could facilitate understanding.

The author draws an analogy to how ALGOL serves as a standard vehicle for describing algorithms and BNF (Backus-Naur Form) for describing language syntax. This RFC proposes a similar standard for defining binary message formats. Rather than diving immediately into bit-level details, the symbolic method first clarifies the overall message structure and alternatives, then adds coding details.
sections.eli5: Instead of drawing bits as little boxes, use words and symbols to describe what a message contains. It is like writing a recipe before trying to cook.

sections.title: The Message Description Language
sections.content:
The proposed format description consists of four declarative sections. First, simple fields are named and described (for example, an OPT field for options, a COORD field for coordinates). Second, field equivalents assign symbolic names to fields with specific values (for example, PHDR as a field OPT with value 2). Third, characterization statements define complex messages using operators: + for concatenation, / for alternatives, =N for repetition, and N: to assign a value to a variable. Fourth, field sizes specify the bit width of each field.

The notation supports conditional fields enclosed in brackets—a field appears only if another field has a particular value—and nested alternatives where the value of one field selects which alternatives follow.
sections.eli5: You name your building blocks (fields), define what each block looks like, show how to stack them together, and then say how wide each block is.

sections.title: Concrete Example
sections.content:
The RFC includes a complete worked example: a format for hierarchical pictorial data. It defines fields like OPT (option, 3 bits), COORD (coordinate, 14 bits), ID (identifier, 9 bits), and COUNT (number of units, 6 bits). It then defines complex structures like POINT (picture header plus coordinate pair), LINE (line header plus two coordinate pairs), and PARTS (a recursive structure of points and lines). Finally, it shows PIXMSG, a complete message that starts with option code 5, followed by a count, that many PIXUNIT structures, and ends with option code 0.

This example demonstrates the notation's power: the message structure is clear from the definitions without any bit-level diagrams, yet the format is precise enough for implementation.
sections.eli5: A real example shows you a message format using the notation, from the high-level structure down to how many bits each piece needs.

sections.title: Vision and Impact
sections.content:
The RFC envisions this notation becoming a standard for documenting network protocols and data formats. It imagines the notation being transmitted in ASCII text over the network itself as standards evolve, and eventually being input to compiler-like programs that automatically generate data translation programs.

While future standards eventually adopted different formal notations and tools, the core insight—that binary formats require explicit, standardized documentation—proved durable. Protocol specifications in all eras since have treated format documentation as central to interoperability.
sections.eli5: Instead of guessing what someone else's message means, read the documented description. This is the beginning of that idea.
